RNA-SEQ & COMPARATIVE GENOMICS · INTERNAL RESEARCH REPORT

HS6 outgrows and outproduces #4
by rewriting two pathways

A fermentation time-course transcriptome comparison of wild-type Schizochytrium sp. #4 against HS6 — developed by EMS mutagenesis plus a carotenoid-synthesis inhibitor, then screened by Nile Red (lipid) and OD (biomass) for higher lipid and growth — cross-checked against the strain's genomic variant record.

● WT · strain #4 ● Mutant · HS6 3 fermentation timepoints · 20h / 44h / 68h 6 libraries, n=1 per condition
Update — reconciled against later comparative-genomics work (2026-07-31)

This report's original causal-mutation search (Section 04) named g6423 and g1760 as the strongest single-gene candidates for the HS6 phenotype. Follow-up work across the wider HS6/#4/#7 comparison (see the HS6 vs. #7 comparative genomics report) found a more systemic candidate: coordinated dysregulation of the MYB3R cell-cycle regulator family (multiple paralogs, both directions) sharing discovered promoter motifs with core lipid-pathway genes (FabD, a fatty-acyl-CoA ligase, and alkane monooxygenase) — see Figure 2, the expression-integrated #4-vs-HS6 map. g6423/g1760 remain plausible contributing mutations but are no longer the leading explanation; the MYB3R/motif finding better accounts for the coordinated, multi-gene expression shift described in Section 03. Separately, the MVK/Scaffolds_28 copy-number duplication highlighted in the HS6-vs-#7 work was checked against this WT(#4) strain's own resequencing data and found to be shared by #4 and HS6 alike — it predates the EMS mutagenesis and does not explain the HS6-vs-#4 difference.

01

What we found

HS6 was bred for faster growth and higher DHA/lipid yield on GYP medium. The transcriptome shows a coherent explanation for both: a reallocation of resources away from cytoskeletal machinery, and a metabolic shift from burning stored lipid toward making more of it via the DHA-specific synthase pathway.

02

The data separate cleanly on both axes

Principal component analysis of all 6 libraries shows fermentation time as the dominant axis of variation, with genotype as a clean secondary axis — the structure a real biological signal should have, before any hypothesis testing.

03

Two pathways explain the phenotype

Gene-level evidence, not just enrichment statistics, points to two coordinated programs.

Lipid & DHA: synthesize more, break down less

HS6 upregulates the DHA-specific polyketide synthase pathway while suppressing the enzymes that mobilize stored triacylglycerol — a "make more, burn less" signature that would directly raise lipid yield.

g15357 Polyketide synthase Pks13 — the DHA-synthesis pathway itself +1.54 log2FC
g8236 Triacylglycerol lipase SDP1 — mobilizes stored lipid -1.33 log2FC
g12095 Malonyl-CoA:ACP transacylase — conventional FAS pathway -1.86 log2FC
g7896 Diacylglycerol O-acyltransferase (DGAT) -2.63 log2FC
g8276 Lipid droplet-associated hydrolase -0.84 log2FC

Growth: less cytoskeleton, faster cycle

Independent myosin and actin paralogs move together and down, alongside the single most significant gene in this category — a cyclin-dependent kinase — moving up.

g1305 Actin -1.92 log2FC
g8048 Myosin-6 -2.04 log2FC
g7259 Myosin-2 -1.74 log2FC
g6428 Myosin-1 -1.76 log2FC
g13536 Cyclin-dependent kinase F-3 — most significant gene in this group +3.36 log2FC

What the whole gene set says, not just the highlights

A third program: dialing down the competing isoprenoid pathway

HS6 was developed by EMS mutagenesis combined with a carotenoid-synthesis inhibitor, then screened by Nile Red fluorescence (lipid) and OD (biomass) — selecting directly for cells that reroute carbon away from carotenoids and into growth and lipid. The transcriptome shows exactly that: g12136, diphosphomevalonate decarboxylase — a rate-limiting enzyme in the mevalonate pathway that supplies isoprenoid precursors to carotenoid synthesis — is significantly down (log2FC=−1.13, padj=2.0×10⁻⁴). Carotenoid and lipid synthesis compete for the same acetyl-CoA–derived carbon pool; suppressing the former is a mechanistically direct way to feed the latter.

Reading the iron signal

Genes up in HS6 are also enriched for iron acquisition (ferric-chelate reductase, iron import). PUFA desaturases and electron-transport steps in DHA synthesis are iron/Fe–S cofactor–dependent, so this may be supporting infrastructure for the increased desaturation flux above — not a separate, unrelated program.

04

Cross-checking against the genome

Schizochytrium HS6 was PacBio HiFi–assembled; #4 was only short-read resequenced against this same HS6 reference — the correct and only viable reference for this project. Two independent variant analyses were run against it.

The existing scan (primary reference)

An existing consensus-diff variant scan in the project folder (not a standard VCF pipeline) found a small mutation load: only 36 genes genome-wide carry a coding change under permissive filtering, 8 under strict filtering.

A rigorous rerun, as corroboration

Using the vendor-validated WT(#4) reads (121× coverage; BWA-MEM alignment matched the vendor's own read count exactly: 49,508,542), a proper haploid-model variant call was run to supplement the scan above. It also explains something the original vendor WGS report couldn't: that report called 3,302 of 3,307 SNPs "heterozygous" — implausible for a haploid microbe. Forcing the correct ploidy (=1) and filtering for clean allele support collapses this to 10 high-confidence, isolated mutations genome-wide (5 SNP, 5 indel) — the rest were misalignment noise in repetitive/homopolymer regions, the same phenomenon behind this project's RNA-seq multi-mapping (§05).

The one convergence point — and it matches the mutagen's own signature

One high-confidence mutation (g14345, intronic, no coding change) falls inside a gene that is itself significantly up in HS6 (log2FC=+0.76, padj=0.033) — the single instance across both variant analyses where a mutation and a transcriptional change land on the same gene. HS6 was developed by EMS treatment, a mutagen with a distinctive, near-exclusive G:C→A:T transition signature. Checked against the correct mutation direction (ancestral WT→derived HS6), this is the only one of the 5 clean SNPs that is a C→T transition matching that signature — the other 4 are transversions, inconsistent with EMS and more likely pre-existing strain polymorphism. It has no SwissProt homolog, so its identity is unknown; this convergence (mutation + EMS signature + transcriptional change) makes it the single strongest candidate for follow-up in this dataset.

Both analyses agree on the headline conclusion: none of the genes actually driving the phenotype — Pks13, SDP1, Actin, the myosin paralogs, CDK F-3 — carry a coding mutation. The transcriptional reprogramming isn't explained by simple coding-sequence breakage in those genes. The more likely explanation is a trans-acting mutation (a regulator whose own sequence changed, cascading to hundreds of downstream genes) or a change outside what short-read SNP/indel calling resolves — the vendor's own structural-variant screen (BreakDancer/Pindel/Delly) found no SV supported by ≥2 methods, so that avenue looks closed too.

Update — two plausible regulators identified via InterProScan

A pre-existing but never-run InterProScan input file was found in the project folder, containing exactly the 29 genes carrying any mutation from the primary 4.SNP scan. Submitting it (EBI InterProScan5) turned up two strong candidates: g6423 (mutated, significantly down, padj=1.9×10⁻²) carries a Ran-GTPase-activating-protein–like domain with confirmed nuclear localization and nucleocytoplasmic transport GO terms — a plausible mechanism for altering nuclear import/export of transcription factors genome-wide. g1760 (mutated, G-type lectin receptor-like) is confirmed by five independent domain databases as a genuine serine/threonine protein kinase — a kinase mutation can rewire downstream transcription without the kinase's own expression changing, which fits its non-significant own padj (0.26). Both are stronger causal candidates than any of the downstream pathway genes.

Worth a paper-trail check

The original vendor WGS report is titled "Chlorella HS6," while this project is Schizochytrium. Genome size (61.55 vs 61.63 Mb) matches closely enough that this looks like a reused report template rather than wrong-species data, and the rigorous rerun above used the same reads and reproduced the vendor's exact raw-read count — but it's worth confirming with the sequencing vendor before this appears in a manuscript.

05

How this was built

fastp trim→
HISAT2 align to HS6→
featureCounts→
DESeq2 (+ NOISeq cross-check)→
DIAMOND vs SwissProt→
clusterProfiler GO enrichment

Design: ~ time + genotype, all 6 samples pooling dispersion across ~13.5k genes. No biological replicates exist (n=1 per genotype×timepoint); genes reported here are prioritized by significance and by directional consistency across all three fermentation timepoints, which is the closest available substitute for replication.

What would break this if unaddressed

  • No replicates: per-gene p-values borrow strength across genes, not from repeated measurements. qRT-PCR on the ~15 genes named above is close to mandatory before this goes to review.
  • Draft, scaffold-level genome: ~51–58% of reads align at all; ~10–18% land on an annotated gene (CDS-only annotation, no UTRs). Consistent across all 6 samples, so it biases magnitude, not the WT vs. HS6 comparison itself — but it belongs in the methods section.
  • Some GO terms are homology artifacts: a few "photosynthesis / chloroplast" terms appear via distant homology only — Schizochytrium isn't photosynthetic. Don't cite those terms literally.
